topic: sub:11|Formulas and equations|Distance, speed, time and stopping distances

parts.latex:
Travis is driving on a highway where the legal speed limit is 110 km/h. Travis sees a kangaroo in the distance and applies the brakes in order to avoid hitting it.

If Travis' reaction time is 1.5 seconds and he travels 50 metres in that time, use calculations to determine whether Travis was driving within the legal limit.

solutions.latex:
Speed in metres per second:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{50}{1.5} &\approx 33.3 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$
Convert to km/h:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Speed} &= \dfrac{33.3 \times 3600}{1000} \\ &\approx 120 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$
Since $120 > 110$, Travis was over the speed limit.
criteria: Converts the speed to km/h, or equivalent merit
Finds the speed in m/s, or equivalent merit

meta.final: Over the speed limit (about 120 km/h > 110 km/h)
meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

parts.latex:
Towns A, B, C, and D are in a straight line.

\exfigure{719_q17_1}

Not to scale

The total distance from A to D is $300$ km.

It takes a car 2 hours 36 minutes to get from town A to town C going at $105$ km/h.

A bike took $24$ minutes to travel from town D to town C.

What was the speed of the bike in km/h?

solutions.latex:
Using $D = S \times T$ for the car, with $T = 2\dfrac{36}{60}$ hours:
$$\begin{aligned} AC &= 105 \times 2\dfrac{36}{60} \\ &= 273 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} CD &= AD - AC \\ &= 300 - 273 \\ &= 27 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
For the bike, $S = \dfrac{D}{T}$ with $T = \dfrac{24}{60}$ hours:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= \dfrac{27}{\frac{24}{60}} \\ &= 67.5 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

parts.latex:
In 2009, Usain Bolt set a world record of 9.58 seconds for the 100 m sprint.

Find his speed in km/h, giving your final answer correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex:
Convert 100 m to $0.1$ km, so he travels $\dfrac{0.1}{9.58}$ km each second.

There are 3600 seconds in an hour:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{speed} &= \dfrac{0.1}{9.58}\times 3600 \\ &= 37.578\ldots \\ &\approx 37.6 \text{ km/h (to 1 decimal place)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Converts to km and seconds to hours correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

parts.latex:
The distance between Bluetown and Green Creek is 100 km.

A person travels from Bluetown to Green Creek at an average speed of 40 km/h.

How long does it take the person to complete the journey ?

solutions.latex:
Using $\text{time} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{time} &= \dfrac{100}{40} \\ &= 2.5 \text{ hours} \\ &= 2 \text{ hours } 30 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$
So the correct option is C.

parts.latex:
When driving his car, Adrian travels $x$ km in 2 hours at a speed of $y$ km/h.

Which of the following represents this information?

solutions.latex:
Speed is distance divided by time. The distance is $x$ km and the time is $2$ hours, so
$$y=\dfrac{x}{2}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
Juliette is driving along the highway at 100 km/h. She notices a possum on the road and applies the brakes 1.6 seconds after noticing the possum. Her braking distance is 98 metres.

What is her approximate stopping distance?

solutions.latex:
Stopping distance is the reaction distance plus the braking distance.

Convert the speed to metres per second.

$$\begin{aligned} 100 \text{ km/h} &= \dfrac{100\times 1000}{3600} \\ &\approx 27.8 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$
The reaction distance is the distance travelled in the 1.6 seconds before braking.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Reaction distance} &\approx 27.8\times 1.6 \\ &\approx 44.4 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Stopping distance} &\approx 44.4 + 98 \\ &\approx 142 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: A train departs from Town A at 3.00 pm to travel to Town B. Its average speed for the journey is 90 km/h, and it arrives at 5.00 pm. A second train departs from Town A at 3.10 pm and arrives at Town B at 4.30 pm. What is the average speed of the second train?

solutions.latex:
The first train travels for 2 hours (3.00 pm to 5.00 pm) at $90$ km/h, using $\text{distance} = \text{speed} \times \text{time}$.
$$\begin{aligned} d &= 90 \times 2 \\ &= 180 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
The second train travels from 3.10 pm to 4.30 pm, which is $80$ minutes $= \dfrac{4}{3}$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{speed} &= \dfrac{180}{\frac{4}{3}} \\ &= 135 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option A.

figures.cap: right-angled triangle circuit with sides 1800 m and 1600 m

solutions.latex:
Let the unknown side be $x$. By Pythagoras' theorem (hypotenuse $1800$ m):
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 1800^2 - 1600^2 \\ &= 680\,000 \\ x &= 824.6211\ldots \end{aligned}$$
The perimeter is
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 824.6211\ldots + 1600 + 1800 \\ &= 4224.62\ldots \text{ m} \\ &= 4.2246\ldots \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
Using $\text{time} = \dfrac{d}{s}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{time} &= \dfrac{4.2246\ldots}{9} \\ &= 0.4694\ldots \text{ h} \\ &= 28.16 \text{ min} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{he will finish his run in under 30 minutes}$$
criteria: Finds the perimeter of the triangle and attempts to use the rate to find the time taken, or equivalent merit
Finds the unknown side length, or uses the two known sides to calculate the time taken, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source typo 4244.62 corrected to 4224.62 m; later values were already consistent. Figure not visible here; Pythagoras assumes 1800 m is the hypotenuse.

parts.latex: Find the average speed of a car that take 2 hours 20 minutes to travel 125 km (correct to 1 decimal place).

solutions.latex:
Convert the time: $2$ hours $20$ minutes $= 2\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3}$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{speed} &= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} \\ &= \dfrac{125}{\frac{7}{3}} \\ &\approx 53.6 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$

meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

parts.latex: The distance between Bricktown and Koala Creek is 75 km. A person travels from Bricktown to Koala Creek at an average speed of 50 km/h. How long does it take the person to complete the journey?

solutions.latex:
Using $\text{time} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{time} &= \dfrac{75}{50} \\ &= 1.5 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
This is 1 hour 30 minutes, so the answer is C.

7123.stem: Grant ran a marathon of 42.194 km in 3 hours 8 minutes.

parts.latex: What was Grant's average speed in km/h, correct to one decimal place?
If Grant ran this constant speed over 400 m, how long would it take him, correct to the nearest second?

solutions.latex:
The time is 3 hours 8 minutes $= 3\dfrac{8}{60}$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Speed} &= \dfrac{42.194}{3\frac{8}{60}} \\ &\approx 13.5 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Lucy is driving on a regional road at a speed of 72 kilometres per hour and must brake suddenly. She has a reaction time of 1.5 seconds and a braking distance of 25 metres.

Stopping distance can be calculated using the following formula

$\text{stopping distance } (d) = \{\text{reaction time distance}\} + \{\text{braking distance}\}$

What is Lucy’s stopping distance in metres?

solutions.latex:
Reaction distance is speed multiplied by time.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Reaction distance} &= s \times t \\ &= \dfrac{72\,000}{3600} \times 1.5 \\ &= 30\text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, $72 \times \dfrac{1.5}{60 \times 60} = 0.03\text{ km} = 30\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Stopping distance} &= 30 + 25 \\ &= 55\text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the reaction distance, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).
meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

parts.latex:
The stopping distance ($S$) in metres of a motor vehicle travelling at $V$ km/h can be modelled by the equation: $S = B + R$ where $B$ is the braking distance (metres) and $R$ is the drivers reaction distance (metres).

If $B = 0.01V^2$ and $R = 0.7V$ what is the stopping distance (metres) of a motor vehicle travelling with a speed of 60 km/h?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $V = 60$ into each formula.
$$\begin{aligned} B &= 0.01 \times 60^2 = 36 \\ R &= 0.7 \times 60 = 42 \end{aligned}$$
Then add the two distances.
$$\begin{aligned} S &= B + R \\ &= 36 + 42 \\ &= 78 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the stopping distance is } 78 \text{ m (option D)}$$

7366.stem:
The emergency stopping distance ($S$) (in metres) required by a motorist on dry surfaces consists of the reaction distance $R$ plus the braking distance $B$ (both in metres), given by the formulas:

$$R = 0.7v,\qquad B = 0.01v^2 \quad \text{and} \quad S = R + B$$

where $v$ is the speed of the vehicle (in km/h).

figures.cap: Stopping Distances on a Dry Surface: graph of B = 0.01v^2 on grid

parts.latex: Show that when a motorist is travelling at 70 km/h on a dry surface, the braking distance and the reaction distance are equal.
What is the stopping distance when travelling at 70 km/h?
If $0.01v^2 = 25$, what is the value of $S$?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $v = 70$ into each formula.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 0.7\times 70 = 49 \text{ m} \\ B &= 0.01\times 70^2 = 0.01\times 4900 = 49 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ R = B = 49 \text{ m at } 70 \text{ km/h}$$
criteria: Correctly finds one of $R$ or $B$, or equivalent merit

meta.generated_note: Written by us; no source solution.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} S &= R + B \\ &= 49 + 49 \\ &= 98 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the stopping distance is } 98 \text{ m}$$

meta.generated_note: Written by us; no source solution.
meta.final_by: claude-sonnet-5-5 26 Nov (read from the worked solution)

solutions.latex:
$R = 0.7v$ is a straight line through the origin. Two points are enough:
$$\begin{aligned} v = 0:&\ R = 0 \\ v = 100:&\ R = 0.7\times 100 = 70 \end{aligned}$$
So the line joins $(0, 0)$ and $(100, 70)$. As a check, it passes through $(70, 49)$, where it meets the braking curve (from part (a)).

\exfigure{235_q30_s1}
criteria: Plots one correct point or draws a straight line through the origin, or equivalent merit

meta.generated_note: Written by us; no source solution.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} 0.01v^2 &= 25 \\ v^2 &= 2500 \\ v &= 50 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$
(the speed is positive). Then
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 0.7\times 50 = 35 \text{ m} \\ S &= R + B = 35 + 25 = 60 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ S = 60 \text{ m}$$

parts.latex:
The current world record for the men's 100-metre sprint is 9.58 seconds set by Usain Bolt, a Jamaican sprinter, in 2009.

Which of the following expresses the rate of Bolt's record-setting sprint in kilometres per hour, correct to one decimal place?

solutions.latex:
Convert the distance to kilometres and the time to hours.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 0.1 \text{ km} \\ \text{Time} &= \dfrac{9.58}{3600} \text{ h} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Speed} &= \dfrac{0.1}{\frac{9.58}{3600}} \\ &\approx 37.6 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the answer is option C}$$

meta.generated_note: MCQ working written for key C

parts.latex: Nick lives in Rochdale and drives to work in Trafford. Determine the length of the shortest path he can travel from home to work.
On each road shown on the diagram, the speed limit is 50km/h. Determine the time taken to travel on this route, given that he travels at the speed limit for the whole journey.

The speed limit along the orbital road is 120km/h. The roads connecting $R$ to $X$ and $R$ to $Y$ both have a speed limit of 60km/h.

How much time will Nick save by driving to work, connecting to and travelling on the orbital road, compared to the quickest route he could have taken using the original roads? Assume that he travels at the speed limit for the whole journey. Give answer in minutes and seconds.

solutions.latex: The shortest path is $R-O-A-S-T$, with length $19$ km.
